summary:
Punjab has no statute of its own targeting transgender people. A trans visitor to Punjab stands under India's national framework. In March 2026 India's Parliament passed the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Amendment Bill, replacing the 2019 law's self-identification route with legal recognition limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner, and to intersex individuals. Trans men, trans women and non-binary people who self-identify outside those categories fall outside the recognition scheme. Rights activists, among them Akkai Padmashali, describe the amendment as criminalising and an attack on the right to exist. The government presents it as widening access to welfare schemes and protection from trafficking, while critics say it excludes many trans, non-binary and gender-fluid people. India has an estimated two million transgender people.

The statute of record in Punjab is the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019 (Act No. 40 of 2019). It was passed by the Lok Sabha on 5 August 2019 and the Rajya Sabha on 26 November 2019, received presidential assent on 5 December 2019, and has been in force since 10 January 2020. Following the Supreme Court's 2014 NALSA judgment, it grants transgender people the right to declare a self-perceived gender identity without undergoing sex reassignment surgery, bans discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, creates a National Council for Transgender Persons, and prescribes imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine for crimes against transgender people. Criticism holds that the Act omits mandatory reservations in jobs and education. On 27 January 2020 the Supreme Court issued notice in a petition challenging the Act's constitutionality.

Determinations that bind Punjab include the Supreme Court's judgment of 6 September 2018 in Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India, in which a five-judge bench ruled unanimously to strike down Section 377 of the Indian Penal Code insofar as it criminalised consensual same-sex acts, holding that discrimination based on sexual orientation violates the Constitution while preserving the provision for non-consensual acts. The 2014 NALSA judgment recognised a legal third gender and the right to self-identified gender identity. In July 2024 the Indian Penal Code was replaced by the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, which omits Section 377 entirely; the replacement also removed gender-identity-specific sexual-violence offences that had protected trans persons under the old code, and trans people fear a rise in assaults as a result. Discrimination is barred on grounds including sex, which courts have interpreted to cover gender identity. There is no same-sex marriage or civil partnership in India, although courts have acknowledged same-sex couples as family units.

Punjab's clearest documented signal is institutional rather than criminal. Pride Amritsar cancelled the parade scheduled for 27 April 2025 at the Rose Garden after mounting resistance from Sikh religious organisations, including the Nihang Singh faction and the Akal Takht, with organisers citing religious-group opposition as the reason. The Washington Blade reported the cancellation on 23 April 2025. No state intervention to preserve the event is recorded in the audited sources, so organised religious opposition has compelled the disappearance of Punjab's annual public trans assembly.

Identity documents and checkpoints are a live source of friction across India. In February 2026 the Allahabad High Court granted relief to a trans person who had been asked to take a medical exam by passport authorities. In November 2024 an openly transgender law student, Sakshi Jain, was stopped at Chennai International Airport Terminal 1 by Central Industrial Security Force personnel despite presenting her PAN card for identity verification. In Kolkata a transwoman alleged that a Railway Protection Force constable groped her at the station under the pretext of checking her gender, and transgender persons arrested by the Railway Protection Force in Assam have recounted degrading treatment in custody.

Assessments of police conduct diverge. The United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note records limited reports of police abuse of LGBT+ people, likelier in conservative rural areas and not systemic, while victim interviews documented in June 2024 record abusive treatment of trans detainees by railway police. The Madras High Court's judgment of 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police issued sweeping guidelines on protecting LGBTQIA+ persons, police sensitisation and a ban on conversion therapy, with directions to the National Medical Commission and education authorities. Bans on conversion therapy from that judgment and from the National Medical Commission in 2022 coexist with clandestine networks still operating.

Nationally the Ayushman Bharat scheme was expanded in April 2024 to cover transition-related healthcare for all members of the transgender community, and in August 2024 the Ministry of Finance clarified that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on opening joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries. Intersex minors remain at risk: reports document a history of infanticide and a strong parental preference for assigning intersex infants male through non-consensual operations, and the Madras High Court ordered Tamil Nadu in April 2019 to ban sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants.
tangentialFactors:
Facilities, welfare boards and care delivery are set largely at state level, and Punjab is not among the states the audited sources name as operating a transgender welfare board. Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha run such boards coordinating housing subsidies, free sex reassignment surgery in public hospitals and pensions, and several states provide targeted welfare, housing and healthcare benefits for hijras. A trans visitor comparing states should expect a materially different service environment in those jurisdictions than in Punjab, where no equivalent state machinery is documented.

The pattern of organised religious opposition to public trans assembly is not unique to Punjab but its outcome there is stark: a cancelled Pride parade with no recorded official counterweight. Where other Indian states have seen state-funded Pride or welfare programming, Punjab's documented trajectory runs the other way, with religious bodies supplying the operative constraint on visibility.

Criminal-law protection weakened nationally in 2024 with the replacement of the Indian Penal Code, so the risk profile in Punjab is shaped by a code that omits the gender-identity-specific offences the old law carried. This sits alongside a 2018 decriminalisation ruling and a 2014 recognition of a third gender, producing a mixed baseline: consensual adult conduct is lawful and identity is legally recognised in principle, while the specific offences trans people had relied on are gone.

The 2019 Act's penalty range for crimes against transgender people, six months to two years plus a fine, is commonly criticised as far below the sentences available for parallel offences against other victims, which affects how protection operates in practice rather than on paper.
localsOnly:
Residents of Punjab hold the rights set out in the Transgender Persons (Protection of Rights) Act, 2019: the right to declare a self-perceived gender identity without sex reassignment surgery, protection from discrimination in education, employment, healthcare and housing, and access to the National Council for Transgender Persons. Following the March 2026 amendment, the route to legal recognition for residents is limited to historically accepted socio-cultural groups such as hijra and kinner and to intersex individuals; residents whose gender identity falls outside those categories are outside the recognition scheme, and the practical effect of that limit on Punjab's residents is not documented in the audited sources.

Residents reporting crimes against transgender persons can invoke the 2019 Act's offence provisions, which carry imprisonment of not less than six months up to two years plus a fine. Punjab's residents are also covered by the Ayushman Bharat expansion of April 2024 for transition-related healthcare, and by the Ministry of Finance clarification of August 2024 that LGBTQ people face no restrictions on joint bank accounts or naming partners as beneficiaries.

Residents seeking police protection can rely on the directions issued by the Madras High Court on 7 June 2021 in S. Sushma v Commissioner of Police, including police sensitisation and the ban on conversion therapy, alongside the National Medical Commission's 2022 ban; clandestine conversion networks nonetheless continue to operate. Residents of Tamil Nadu, by contrast, hold a state-level intersex protections order from April 2019 banning sex-selective surgeries on intersex infants, for which no Punjab equivalent is documented.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved and not sourced: whether Punjab operates any state-level transgender welfare board, housing subsidy, pension or public-hospital surgery programme. The audited sources name Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Maharashtra and Odisha as running such boards and record Punjab's absence from that list, but do not state affirmatively that Punjab has none.

Unresolved and not sourced: how the March 2026 amendment is administered in Punjab in practice, including which authority issues recognition certificates, what evidence is demanded of applicants, and whether any Punjab resident has been refused recognition under the amended criteria. No Punjab-specific enforcement, arrest, prosecution or conviction data under the 2019 Act's offence provisions appears in the audited sources.

Unresolved and not sourced: whether the 27 January 2020 constitutional challenge to the 2019 Act has been decided, and what the amended statute's status is in relation to that petition. The audited sources record only the issuance of notice.

Unresolved and not sourced: whether any police unit in Punjab has faced proceedings over mistreatment of trans detainees, and whether the Madras High Court's 2021 sensitisation directions have been implemented by Punjab police. The two available assessments of Indian police conduct, the United Kingdom's December 2025 country policy note and the June 2024 victim interviews on railway police, are national in scope and do not disaggregate Punjab.
